definition: TypeScript's rule that a value is compatible with a type when it has the required shape, whatever the type is called. Two differently named types with the same properties are interchangeable.
Whether a value of one type can be used where another type is expected. It works like the subset relation: a narrower set of values fits into a wider one.
A check that flags unknown properties in a fresh object literal written directly where a type is expected. It catches typos, but values passed through a variable skip it.
How TypeScript tracks the type of a variable through branches, returns and assignments, so the same name can have a narrower type after a check than before it.
Refining a wide type to a more specific one with a runtime check such as `typeof`, `===`, `in`, `instanceof` or a type predicate.
A union of object types that share a property with a different literal value in each member, such as `status`. Checking that property narrows the whole object to one member.
A const assertion that infers the narrowest type for a value: literals stay literal, arrays become readonly tuples and properties become readonly.
An operator that checks a value against a type without replacing the value's inferred type, so you get validation and keep precise keys and literals.
A placeholder type in a generic function or type, such as `T`, that links inputs to outputs. It should appear at least twice to add real type safety.
An `extends` clause on a type parameter that limits which types it accepts, such as `T extends { id: number }`, which also makes those properties usable inside the function.
A position in a parameter type where a type parameter appears. At a call, TypeScript collects a candidate from each site to decide what the type parameter is.
A type parameter declared with `const` (TypeScript 5.0+), which infers arguments as if the caller had written `as const`, keeping literals and readonly tuples.
A built-in type (TypeScript 5.4+) that marks a position as check-only, so it is validated against a type parameter but never contributes an inference candidate.
A type such as `Order['status']` or `T[number]` that looks up the type of a property, or of an array's elements, using bracket syntax.
A type that loops over a union of keys and builds one property per key, as in `{ [K in keyof T]?: T[K] }`, the definition of `Partial`.
An `as` clause in a mapped type that renames each key, often with a template literal. Mapping a key to `never` removes it, which is how `Omit` works.
A type of the form `T extends U ? X : Y` that chooses between two types depending on whether `T` is assignable to `U`.
A conditional type whose checked type is a naked type parameter. Given a union, it runs once per member and joins the results; wrapping both sides in brackets turns this off.
A keyword used inside the `extends` clause of a conditional type to capture part of a matched type, as in `ReturnType`, which captures a function's return type.
A string type built with backtick syntax from other types, such as `` `order.${OrderStatus}` ``. Unions inside it expand into every combination.
A primitive intersected with a type-only property, such as `number & { readonly [brand]: 'OrderId' }`, so values with the same runtime type stop being interchangeable.
A function that validates a raw value and returns it as a branded type. It is the only place a cast to the brand should appear.
A compile-time guarantee that every member of a union is handled, usually by passing the leftover value to a parameter of type `never` in a `default` branch.
A discriminated union such as `{ ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: E }` that returns expected failures as values, so callers must handle them.
A function return type of the form `value is T`. When the function returns true, the argument is narrowed to `T` at the call site; the body itself is not verified.
A function whose return type is `asserts value is T`. It throws when the check fails and narrows the value for the rest of the scope when it returns.
A declaration that calls the value's `[Symbol.dispose]()` method when its block exits, by return or by throw, disposing several resources in reverse order.
The rule that several declarations with the same name, such as two interfaces, combine into one. It is how you extend lib types and library interfaces.
Adding to the types inside a module with `declare module 'name' { … }` from a file that is itself a module, for example to extend a library's interface.
A tsconfig feature that splits a codebase into separately built projects (`composite: true`, built with `tsc -b`), so unchanged parts are not re-checked.
